readings.title: A drawing class with mixed experience
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An arts centre welcomed adults to a drawing class. Beginners felt lost when the tutor began with a complicated still-life exercise. The main obstacle was one task for learners at different stages. Experienced participants finished quickly while newcomers hesitated over basic materials. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used feedback after two trial lessons. The tutor asked students which steps they could repeat without help. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a common theme could allow different difficulty levels. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced two task paths and a short materials demonstration. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: inclusive teaching preserves challenge and support. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a drawing class with mixed experience, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A concert in a small hall
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A youth orchestra played in a hall with poor sight lines. People at the back heard the music but could not see the conductor. The main obstacle was seating arranged only by ticket order. Tall equipment near the front blocked the view from several ordinary seats. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a view check from each seating row. Organizers sat at different heights and noted which objects interrupted the stage. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated moving equipment solved much of the problem. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised seating plan with clear sight lines. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: audience experience involves more than sound. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in a concert in a small hall, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Labels for a community exhibition
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A gallery displayed paintings by local residents. Visitors enjoyed the pictures but wanted to know how artists chose their subjects. The main obstacle was labels listing names but little context. The existing cards gave dates and materials without explaining personal stories. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used short interviews with participating artists. Curators asked artists what they wished visitors to notice and edited answers with consent. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated brief artist voices enriched viewing. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced optional short stories beside each work. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: context can make art more approachable. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in labels for a community exhibition, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Rehearsing a public play
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A local theatre group rehearsed after work. Some members missed changes because notes appeared in several different chat threads. The main obstacle was updates scattered across conversations. Actors could not tell which script version or rehearsal time was current. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a review of missed rehearsal messages. The director compared communication channels and asked members where they looked first. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated one dated notice reduced uncertainty. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a single schedule and versioned script link. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: creative collaboration still needs clear records. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in rehearsing a public play, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for arts activities and education must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the community arts education programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于艺术活动与教育的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the arts learning team about a community activity related to arts activities and education. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community arts education programme. People have noticed one task for learners at different stages, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
